paragraphs: I experienced a four-week clinical clerkship in neurology and breast and endocrine surgery at Korea University in South Korea. Before I left I was anxious about differences in language and culture, but through the clerkship I gained valuable experience and learned a great deal. I would like to report on it below.

Korea University, where I did the clerkship, is a prestigious university located in Seoul, the capital of South Korea. Life in the city of Seoul was very convenient, public transport is well developed, and commuting to the hospital and getting around the city were smooth. Also, because eating-out culture is thriving, I could enjoy various Korean dishes. Since I could not stay in the university dormitory, I rented a studio apartment a little away from the university, but there were a large supermarket and convenience stores nearby, and I felt no inconvenience in daily life. As for Korean, I had studied words at the level of everyday conversation beforehand, but during the clerkship I had no opportunity to interact directly with patients, and communication with doctors and students was mainly in English.

In neurology I mainly learned about diseases such as stroke and dementia. In addition to lectures and rounds by the supervising doctors, discussions and presentations among students were also held, and I gained two-way learning. In watching a film about dementia followed by discussion, and receiving a lecture on interventions for cerebral infarction, my understanding deepened of the differences between Japanese and Korean medicine and of the social background surrounding healthcare. In breast and endocrine surgery I mainly observed operations, and also did outpatient observation and took part in conferences. I was allowed to observe a wide range of cases, such as total mastectomy and partial resection for breast cancer, open neck surgery for thyroid tumors, and robot-assisted surgery. Also, at conferences and at a meal with the supervising doctor, I was able to exchange opinions about the differences in healthcare systems and training systems between Korea and Japan, which was a very meaningful time.

During the clerkship I was able to touch Korean student culture through lunches with local medical students and joining a local tennis circle. Although I could not yet speak Korean well, many Korean students were used to English and actively supported me, so I was able to interact smoothly.

Through this clinical clerkship at Korea University, I realized the importance not only of medical knowledge and skills but also of understanding other cultures and international communication ability. Although it was a short period, the experience of learning medicine overseas became an opportunity that greatly broadened my horizons. I sincerely thank everyone at Nagoya University and Korea University who provided this valuable opportunity. From now on I will make use of this experience and work even harder so that I can grow as a doctor with an international perspective.
